{{Nihongo|'''''Kyōgen'''''|狂言|extra="mad words" or "wild speech"}} is a form of traditional [[:en:Japan|Japan]]ese comic [[:en:Theater|Theater]]. It developed alongside ''[[:en:Noh|Noh]]'', was performed along with ''Noh'' as an intermission of sorts between ''Noh'' acts on the same stage, and retains close links to ''Noh'' in the modern day; therefore, it is sometimes designated '''''Noh-kyōgen'''''. Its contents are nevertheless not at all similar to the formal, symbolic, and solemn ''Noh'' theater; ''kyōgen'' is a comic form, and its primary goal is to make its audience laugh.
''Kyōgen'' together with ''Noh'' is part of ''[[:en:Nōgaku|Nōgaku]]'' theatre.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/nogaku-theatre-00012|title=Nôgaku theatre - intangible heritage - Culture Sector - UNESCO|website=ich.unesco.org|access-date=29 April 2018}}</ref>
''Kyōgen'' is sometimes compared to the Italian comic form of [[:en:commedia dell'arte|commedia dell'arte]]<ref>https://journals.library.brandeis.edu%2Findex.php%2FPMAJLS%2Farticle%2Fdownload%2F2351%2F1841%2F5834&psig=AOvVaw3u7L8po-EoB3i6zHVdejYq&ust=1730774138655000&source=images&cd=vfe&opi=89978449&ved=0CAYQrpoMahcKEwjwv7a00sGJAxUAAAAAHQAAAAAQBA</ref>, which developed in the early 17h century, and likewise features [[:en:Stock character|Stock character]]s. It also has parallels with the Greek [[:en:satyr play|satyr play]], a short, comical play performed between tragedies.
==History== One of the oldest ancestors of kyogen is considered to be a comical mimicry, which was one of the arts constituting Sangaku ([[:ja:散楽]]), and Sangaku was introduced to Japan from China in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] in the 8th century. In the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (794－1185), sangaku developed into [[:en:Sarugaku|Sarugaku]] by merging with Japanese traditional performing arts such as [[:en:Dengaku|Dengaku]], and in the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (1185－1333), it was divided into Noh, which was a drama of serious singing and dancing, and kyogen, which was a comical speech and play. When [[:en:Kan'ami|Kan'ami]] and [[:en:Zeami Motokiyo|Zeami]] completed Noh in the style known today in the early [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] (1333－1573) in the 14th century, Kyōgen was a simple and comical short play different from the style known today, and performers of kyōgen were under the control of a Noh troupe. In the late Muromachi period, kyōgen as a form of theater was developed and the [[:en:Ōkura school|Ōkura school]] was established by kyōgen performers. In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1606－1868), Sagi school and Izumi school were established. Since the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] designated kyōgen and Noh as ceremonial arts in the Edo period, kyōgen performers of these three schools were employed by the Tokugawa shogunate, each [[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]] (feudal lord) and the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial Court]], and kyōgen also developed greatly.<ref name = "kotobank">[https://web.archive.org/web/20210427204341/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%8B%82%E8%A8%80-52582 Kotobank, ''Kyōgen''.] [[:en:The Asahi Shimbun|The Asahi Shimbun]]</ref>
Kyōgen provided a major influence on the later development of [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] theater. After the earlier, more ribald forms of kabuki had been outlawed in the mid-17th century, the government permitted the establishment of the new ''yarō-kabuki'' (men's kabuki) only on the grounds that it refrain from the previous kabuki forms' lewdness and instead model itself after kyōgen.<ref name = "kotobank"/>
Noh had been the official entertainment form of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], and was therefore subsidized by the government. Kyōgen, performed in conjunction with Noh, also received the patronage of the government and the upper class during this time. Following the [[Meiji Restoration]], however, this support ceased. Without government support, Noh and kyōgen went into decline, as many Japanese citizens gravitated toward the more "modern" Western art forms. In 1879, however, then-former [[:en:President of the United States|US President]] [[:en:Ulysses S. Grant|Ulysses S. Grant]] and his wife, while touring Japan, expressed an interest in the traditional art of Noh. They became the first [[:en:United States|Americans]] to witness Noh and kyōgen plays and are said to have enjoyed the performance. Their approval is believed to have sparked a revival of interest in these forms.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.prweb.com/releases/2004/11/prweb182046.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041223132719/http://www.prweb.com/releases/2004/11/prweb182046.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 23, 2004 |title="First Noh & Kyogen Program Witnessed by Americans" in Boston December 7, 2004. |date= 25 November 2004 |publisher=PRWeb |access-date=31 May 2010}}</ref>
In modern Japan, kyōgen is performed both separately and as a part of Noh. When performed as part of a Noh performance, kyōgen can take three forms: a separate (comic) kyōgen play, performed between two Noh plays (inter-Noh), which is known as {{Nihongo||本狂言|honkyōgen|actual kyōgen}}, as a (non-comic) scene ''within'' a Noh play (intra-Noh, between two scenes), which is known as {{Nihongo||間狂言|'''{{visible anchor|aikyōgen}}'''|in-between kyōgen, kyōgen interval}}, or as {{Nihongo||別狂言|betsukyōgen|special kyōgen}}.
In aikyōgen, most often the main Noh actor (''shite'') leaves the stage and is replaced by a {{Nihongo|kyōgen actor|狂言方|kyōgen-kata}}, who then explains the play (for the benefit of the audience), though other forms are also possible – the aikyōgen happening at the start, or the kyōgen actor otherwise interacting with the Noh actors. As part of Noh, aikyōgen is ''not'' comic – the manner (movements, way of speech) and costume are serious and dramatic. However, the actor is dressed in a kyōgen outfit and uses kyōgen-style language and delivery (rather than Noh language and delivery) – meaning simpler, less archaic language, delivered closer to a speaking voice – and thus can generally be understood by the audience, hence the role in explaining the play. Thus, while the costume and delivery are kyōgen-''style'' (kyōgen in ''form''), the clothing will be more elegant and the delivery less playful than in separate, comic kyōgen. Before and after aikyōgen, the kyōgen actor waits (kneeling in [[:en:Seiza|Seiza]]) at the {{Nihongo|kyogen seat|狂言座|kyōgen-za}} at the end of the bridge (''hashigakari''), close to the stage.
The traditions of kyōgen are maintained primarily by family groups, especially the [[Izumi school]] and [[:en:Ōkura school|Ōkura school]].
==Elements== Kyōgen plays are invariably brief – often about 10 minutes, as traditionally performed between acts of Noh – and often contain only two or three roles, which are often [[:en:Stock character|Stock character]]s. Notable ones include {{Nihongo||太郎冠者|Tarō kaja|main servant, literally "firstborn son + servant"}}, {{Nihongo||次郎冠者|Jirō kaja|second servant, literally "second son + servant"}}, and {{Nihongo|the master|主人|shujin}}.
Movements and dialogue in kyōgen are typically very exaggerated, making the action of the play easy to understand. Elements of [[:en:slapstick|slapstick]] or [[:en:satire|satire]] are present in most kyōgen plays. Some plays are parodies of actual [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] or [[Shinto]] religious rituals; others are shorter, more lively, simplified versions of Noh plays, many of which are derived from [[:en:Japanese folktales|folktales]]. As with Noh, [[:en:Jo-ha-kyū|Jo-ha-kyū]] is a fundamental principle, which is particularly relevant for movement.
As with Noh and kabuki, all kyōgen [[:en:actor|actor]]s, including those in female roles, are men. Female roles are indicated by a particular piece of attire, a {{Nihongo||美男鬘|binankazura}} – a long white sash, wrapped around the head, with the ends hanging down the front of the body and tucked into the belt, like symbolic braids; at the two points (either side of the head) where the sash changes from being wrapped around to hanging down, the sash sticks up, like two small horns.
Similarly, actors play roles regardless of age – an old man may play the role of Tarō kaja opposite a young man playing master, for instance.
=== Costumes === Outfits are generally [[:en:Kamishimo|Kamishimo]] (Edo period outfit consisting of [[:en:Kataginu|Kataginu]] top and [[:en:Hakama|Hakama]] pants), with the master (if present) generally wearing [[nagabakama]] (long, trailing pants).
Actors in kyōgen, unlike those in Noh, typically do not wear masks, unless the role is that of an animal (such as a [[:en:Bake-danuki|tanuki]] or [[:en:Kitsune|Kitsune]]), or that of a god. Consequently, the masks of kyōgen are less numerous in variety than Noh masks. Both masks and costumes are simpler than those characteristic of Noh. Few props are used, and minimal or no stage sets. As with Noh, a fan is a common accessory.
=== Language === The language in kyōgen depends on the period, but much of the classic repertoire is in [[:en:Early Modern Japanese|Early Modern Japanese]], reasonably analogous to [[:en:Early Modern English|Early Modern English]] (as in [[:en:Shakespeare|Shakespeare]]). The language is largely understandable to contemporary Japanese speakers, but sounds archaic, with pervasive use of the {{Nihongo||ござる|gozaru}} form rather than the {{Nihongo||ます|masu}} form that is now used (see [[Copula (linguistics)#Japanese|copula: Japanese]]). For example, when acknowledging a command, Tarō kaja often replies with {{Nihongo||畏まってござる|kashikomatte-gozaru|"Yes sir!"}}, which in modern Japanese one uses {{Nihongo||畏まりました|kashikomarimashita}}. Further, some of the words and nuances cannot be understood by modern audience (without notes), as in Shakespeare. This contrasts with Noh, where the language is more difficult and generally not understandable to a contemporary audience.
There are numerous set patterns – stock phrases and associated gestures, such as ''kashikomatte-gozaru'' (with a bow) and ''Kore wa mazu nanto itasō. Iya! Itashiyō ga gozaru.'' "So first, what to do. Aha! There is a way to do it.", performed while bowing and cocking head (indicating thought), followed by standing up with a start on ''Iya!'' Plays often begin with set phrases such as ''Kore wa kono atari ni sumai-itasu mono de gozaru.'' "This is the person who resides in this place." and (if featuring Tarō kaja) often end with Tarō kaja running off the stage yelling ''Yaru-mai zo, yaru-mai zo!'' "I won't do it, I won't do it!".
Lines are delivered in a characteristic rhythmic, sing-song voice, and generally quite loudly. Pace, pitch, and volume are all varied for emphasis and effect.
=== Movements === [[File:Noh-stage.jpg|thumb|A contemporary Noh theatre with indoor roofed structure]] As with Noh, which is performed on the same stage, and indeed many martial arts (such as [[:en:Kendo|Kendo]] and [[:en:Aikido|Aikido]]) actors move via {{Nihongo||摺り足|[[suriashi]]}}, sliding their feet, avoiding steps on the easily vibrated Noh stage. When walking, the body seeks to remain at the same level, without bobbing up or down. Plays also frequently feature stamping feet or otherwise hitting the ground (such as jumping) to take advantage of the stage.
As with Noh, angle of gaze is important, and usually a flat gaze is used (avoiding looking down or up, which create a sad or fierce atmosphere, which is to be avoided). Characters usually face each other when speaking, but turn towards the audience when delivering a lengthy speech.
Arms and legs are kept slightly bent. Unless involved in action, hands are kept on upper thighs, with fingers together and thumb tucked in – they move down to the sides of the knees when bowing.
=== Music === Kyōgen is performed to the accompaniment of music, especially the flute, drums, and gong. However, the emphasis of kyōgen is on dialogue and action, rather than on music or dance.
=== Space === Kyogen is generally performed on a Noh stage, as the stage is an important part of the play (the space, the reaction to stamps, the ease of sliding, etc.). It can, however, be performed in any space (particularly by amateur or younger performers), though if possible a Noh-like floor will be installed.
==Komai== In addition to the kyōgen plays themselves, performances include short dances called {{Nihongo||小舞|komai|small dance}}. These are traditional dramatic dances (not comic), performed to a chanted accompaniment, and with varied themes. The movements are broadly similar to Noh dances. The often archaic language used in the lyrics and the chanted delivery means that these chants are often not understandable to a contemporary audience.
==Kyōgen today== Today, kyōgen is performed and practiced regularly, both in major cities (especially Tokyo and Osaka) and throughout the country, and is featured on cultural television programs. In addition to the performances during Noh plays, it is also performed independently, generally in programs of three to five plays.
New kyogen are written regularly, though few new plays enter the repertoire. Particularly significant is {{Nihongo||濯ぎ川|Susugigawa|''The Washing River''}}, written and directed by [[:en:Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki]] in 1953, during his [[Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|post-Kabuki theater work]]. Based on a medieval French farce, this play became the first new ''kyōgen'' to enter the traditional repertoire in a century.<ref>Salz, p.131–136.</ref> In rare cases bilingual kyōgen or fusion of kyōgen with Western forms has been done. An early example is the group ''Mei-no-kai,'' consisting of kyōgen, Noh, and [[:en:shingeki|shingeki]] actors, who staged Beckett's ''[[:en:Waiting for Godot|Waiting for Godot]]'' in 1973; the kyōgen acting was best received.<ref>''The International Reception of Samuel Beckett,'' by Matthew Feldman, "Beckett's Reception in Japan", [https://books.google.com/books?id=cD1B-PzxDckC&pg=PA153 p. 153]</ref> A notable example is the Noho Theatre group, based in Kyoto, under the direction of American Jonah Salz and primary acting by Akira Shigeyama. This group has performed a bilingual Japanese/English translation of ''Susugigawa'' termed ''The Henpecked Husband,'' together with works by [[:en:Samuel Beckett|Samuel Beckett]], notably the mime ''[[:en:Act Without Words I|Act Without Words I]],'' performed by a kyōgen actor in Japanese theatrical style (first performed 1981).<ref name="twist">{{Cite web | title = Noho Theatre: Kyogen with a twist | work = The Japan Times Online | date = Dec 12, 2001 | first = Catherine | last = Pawasarat | access-date = 2012-07-26 | url = http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ft20011212a4.html }}</ref><ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mFkrdBwhvMM Noho Theatre Group ACT WITHOUT WORDS 1], video</ref><ref>"[http://theater.nytimes.com/mem/theater/treview.html?res=9A0DE3DD1538F931A25750C0A960948260 Theater: Beckett, in Japanese Style]", Mel Gussow, ''The New York Times,'' March 12, 1986</ref> This latter features kyōgen movements and Japanese cultural adaptations – for example, the nameless character contemplates suicide not by holding scissors to his throat (as per stage directions), but to his stomach, as if contemplating [[:en:hara-kiri|hara-kiri]]. Unusually for a Beckett adaptation, which are usually strictly controlled by Beckett and his estate, this was presented to Beckett and met with his approval.
The distinctive diction of kyōgen is also occasionally used in other media, with kyōgen actors working as voice actors. An example is the animated movie {{Nihongo|''[[:en:A Country Doctor (film)|A Country Doctor]]''|カフカ 田舎医者|Kafuka: Inaka Isha}} by [[:en:Kōji Yamamura|Kōji Yamamura]], based on "[[:en:A Country Doctor (short story)|A Country Doctor]]" by [[:en:Franz Kafka|Franz Kafka]], where the voices are performed by the Shigeyama family.
As with Noh, many Japanese are familiar with kyōgen only through learning about it in school or television performances. A play frequently featured in textbooks is {{Nihongo||附子|Busu|''The Delicious Poison''}}, where the servants Tarō-kaja and Jirō-kaja are entrusted with some sugar by their master, but told not to eat it, as it is poison; naturally, they eat it. As with Noh, many professional performers are born into a family, often starting performing at a young age, but others are not born into families and beginning practicing in high school or college. Unlike Noh drama or nihonbuyō dance, who earn their living primarily via teaching and support from underlings in the [[:en:Iemoto|Iemoto]] system, but similar to [[rakugo]] comedy, professional kyōgen players earn their living from performing (possibly supplemented by side jobs), and maintain an active touring schedule. Due to the limited repertoire (a classical canon, of which many are no longer performed due to being dated, and few new plays enter) and frequent performances, a professional kyōgen actor can be expected to be familiar with all roles in all plays in their school's repertoire, and to perform them with some regularity.
While there are a number of kyōgen families, there are at present two leading families: the Nomura 野村 family of Tokyo (traditionally Edo region), and the Shigeyama 茂山 family of Kyoto (traditionally [[:en:Kamigata|Kamigata]] region) of the [[:en:Ōkura school|Ōkura school]],<ref name="woodworth">{{Cite web| title = Kyougen: Farce and Folly on the Stage| author = Joseph Woodworth| work = AJET.net - Voice Online| access-date = 2012-07-26| url = http://voice.ajet.net/2010/09/08/kyougen-farce-and-folly-on-the-stage/| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140720134843/http://voice.ajet.net/2010/09/08/kyougen-farce-and-folly-on-the-stage/| archive-date = 2014-07-20}}</ref> both of which are often featured performing on TV, appear in the news, and tour overseas, and have been involved in popularizing and some efforts at modernizing kyōgen.<ref>{{Cite news | issn = 0362-4331| last = Pareles| first = Jon| title = Stage: Nomura Kyogen Theater of Japan| work = The New York Times| access-date = 2012-07-26| date = 1984-07-21| url = https://www.nytimes.com/1984/07/21/arts/stage-nomura-kyogen-theater-of-japan.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title = Revitalized kyogen to a crossroads | work = The Japan Times Online| access-date = 2012-07-26| date = Nov 14, 2001| first = Nobuko| last = Tanaka| url = http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ft20011114a1.html}}</ref> See also the [[:en:List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)|List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)]], whose kyōgen members feature individuals from these families, among others.
=== Foreign actors === In the post-war period, foreigners have participated in kyōgen as amateur performers. A notable early example was the 1956 performance by scholar and translator [[:en:Donald Keene|Donald Keene]] in the play {{Nihongo||千鳥|Chidori|''Plover''}} with [[:en:Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki]] in the role of the [[sake]] shop owner, before an audience including such prominent authors as [[:en:Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|Tanizaki]], [[:en:Yasunari Kawabata|Yasunari Kawabata]] and [[:en:Yukio Mishima|Yukio Mishima]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Keene|first=Donald|author-link=Donald Keene|title=25. Triumph as Tarokaja |url=http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/features/essay/20060708dy02.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20060720051850/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/features/essay/20060708dy02.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 20, 2006|publisher=[[:en:Yomiuri Shimbun|Yomiuri Shimbun]]|date=July 8, 2006|access-date=4 January 2008}}</ref> This is featured in his series of essays, ''Chronicles of My Life in the 20th Century'', and inspired the title of his anthology ''The Blue-Eyed Tarokaja: A Donald Keene Anthology.'' Today foreigners (resident in Japan, with sufficient Japanese skills) are able to practice with amateur troupes.<ref name="woodworth" /> In addition, since 1985, an intensive summer program (originally 6 weeks, now 3 weeks) in kyōgen for beginners has been run at the [[:en:Kyoto Art Center|Kyoto Art Center]], taught by Akira Shigeyama (of the Shigeyama family) and others, and organized by scholar of Japanese theater Jonah Salz.<ref name="twist" /><ref>[https://archive.today/20121219230353/http://en.kac.or.jp/Category:kk]][[Category/46 T.T.T. Category:kk]][[Category] at the [http://en.kac.or.jp/ Kyoto Art Center] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20121219125720/http://en.kac.or.jp/ |date=2012-12-19 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title = Traditional Theatre Training in Kyoto | author = Paura Chan | work = [http://shinpaideshou.wordpress.com/ What can I do with a B.A. in Japanese Studies?] | date = April 5, 2011 | access-date = 2012-07-26 | url = http://shinpaideshou.wordpress.com/2011/04/05/traditional-theatre-training-in-kyoto/}}</ref>
==Plays== There are a few hundred plays in the repertoire (about 180 in the Okura school), but many are now rarely performed, as the audience will not understand the jokes, or would deem them offensive (e.g., for making fun of a blind money-lender).<ref>Don Kenny - The Kyōgen book: an anthology of Japanese classical comedies'' 1989 Demon Plays Asahina (Asahina, the Warrior) Bakuchijuo (A Gambler Beats the King of Hell) Bakuro (Bakuro, the Horse Trainer) Kaminari (Thunder) Kubihiki (Neck Pulling) Oni no Mamako* (The Demon's Stepchild) Seirai (Seirai, the Hawk ...</ref>
Plays commonly studied and performed by beginners, due to brevity and simplicity, include {{Nihongo||痿痢|Shibiri|"Cramps", "Pins and Needles"}}, 舟船, 土筆, 以呂波, and {{Nihongo||口真似|Kuchimane|The Mimic}}.<ref>[http://www.tarokaja.com/wiki.cgi?page=%E1%DF%CE%A1 痿痢]{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ''Shibiri'' "Cramps"</ref> ''Kuchimane'' in particular is frequently performed. Another well-known play, featured in textbooks, is {{Nihongo||附子|Busu|"Wolfsbane", "The Delicious Poison"}}, mentioned above.
Another play is {{Nihongo2|柿山伏}} (''Kakiyamabushi'' or "Persimmon Mountain Hermit"), about an ascetic priest who hungers in the mountains; he uncovers and eats from a persimmon tree, which belongs to a farmer. The farmer catches him in the act and makes a fool out of the priest – getting the priest to pretend to be a crow, a monkey, and a large bird, causing him to fall from the tree. The priest later gets his revenge by chanting and summoning supernatural forces. But in the end, the farmer refuses to nurse the priest back to health.

{{Nihongo|'''''Kyōgen'''''|狂言|extra="mad words" or "wild speech"}} is a form of traditional [[:en:Japan|Japan]]ese comic [[:en:Theater|Theater]]. It developed alongside ''[[:en:Noh|Noh]]'', was performed along with ''Noh'' as an intermission of sorts between ''Noh'' acts on the same stage, and retains close links to ''Noh'' in the modern day; therefore, it is sometimes designated '''''Noh-kyōgen'''''. Its contents are nevertheless not at all similar to the formal, symbolic, and solemn ''Noh'' theater; ''kyōgen'' is a comic form, and its primary goal is to make its audience laugh.
''Kyōgen'' together with ''Noh'' is part of ''[[:en:Nōgaku|Nōgaku]]'' theatre.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/nogaku-theatre-00012|title=Nôgaku theatre - intangible heritage - Culture Sector - UNESCO|website=ich.unesco.org|access-date=29 April 2018}}</ref>
''Kyōgen'' is sometimes compared to the Italian comic form of [[:en:commedia dell'arte|commedia dell'arte]]<ref>https://journals.library.brandeis.edu%2Findex.php%2FPMAJLS%2Farticle%2Fdownload%2F2351%2F1841%2F5834&psig=AOvVaw3u7L8po-EoB3i6zHVdejYq&ust=1730774138655000&source=images&cd=vfe&opi=89978449&ved=0CAYQrpoMahcKEwjwv7a00sGJAxUAAAAAHQAAAAAQBA</ref>, which developed in the early 17h century, and likewise features [[:en:Stock character|Stock character]]s. It also has parallels with the Greek [[:en:satyr play|satyr play]], a short, comical play performed between tragedies.
==History== One of the oldest ancestors of kyogen is considered to be a comical mimicry, which was one of the arts constituting Sangaku ([[:ja:散楽]]), and Sangaku was introduced to Japan from China in the [[:en:Nara period|Nara period]] in the 8th century. In the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (794－1185), sangaku developed into [[:en:Sarugaku|Sarugaku]] by merging with Japanese traditional performing arts such as [[:en:Dengaku|Dengaku]], and in the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]] (1185－1333), it was divided into Noh, which was a drama of serious singing and dancing, and kyogen, which was a comical speech and play. When [[:en:Kan'ami|Kan'ami]] and [[:en:Zeami Motokiyo|Zeami]] completed Noh in the style known today in the early [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] (1333－1573) in the 14th century, Kyōgen was a simple and comical short play different from the style known today, and performers of kyōgen were under the control of a Noh troupe. In the late Muromachi period, kyōgen as a form of theater was developed and the [[:en:Ōkura school|Ōkura school]] was established by kyōgen performers. In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1606－1868), Sagi school and Izumi school were established. Since the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] designated kyōgen and Noh as ceremonial arts in the Edo period, kyōgen performers of these three schools were employed by the Tokugawa shogunate, each [[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]] (feudal lord) and the [[:en:Imperial House of Japan|Imperial Court]], and kyōgen also developed greatly.<ref name = "kotobank">[https://web.archive.org/web/20210427204341/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%8B%82%E8%A8%80-52582 Kotobank, ''Kyōgen''.] [[:en:The Asahi Shimbun|The Asahi Shimbun]]</ref>
Kyōgen provided a major influence on the later development of [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] theater. After the earlier, more ribald forms of kabuki had been outlawed in the mid-17th century, the government permitted the establishment of the new ''yarō-kabuki'' (men's kabuki) only on the grounds that it refrain from the previous kabuki forms' lewdness and instead model itself after kyōgen.<ref name = "kotobank"/>
Noh had been the official entertainment form of the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], and was therefore subsidized by the government. Kyōgen, performed in conjunction with Noh, also received the patronage of the government and the upper class during this time. Following the [[Meiji Restoration]], however, this support ceased. Without government support, Noh and kyōgen went into decline, as many Japanese citizens gravitated toward the more "modern" Western art forms. In 1879, however, then-former [[:en:President of the United States|US President]] [[:en:Ulysses S. Grant|Ulysses S. Grant]] and his wife, while touring Japan, expressed an interest in the traditional art of Noh. They became the first [[:en:United States|Americans]] to witness Noh and kyōgen plays and are said to have enjoyed the performance. Their approval is believed to have sparked a revival of interest in these forms.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.prweb.com/releases/2004/11/prweb182046.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041223132719/http://www.prweb.com/releases/2004/11/prweb182046.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 23, 2004 |title="First Noh & Kyogen Program Witnessed by Americans" in Boston December 7, 2004. |date= 25 November 2004 |publisher=PRWeb |access-date=31 May 2010}}</ref>
In modern Japan, kyōgen is performed both separately and as a part of Noh. When performed as part of a Noh performance, kyōgen can take three forms: a separate (comic) kyōgen play, performed between two Noh plays (inter-Noh), which is known as {{Nihongo||本狂言|honkyōgen|actual kyōgen}}, as a (non-comic) scene ''within'' a Noh play (intra-Noh, between two scenes), which is known as {{Nihongo||間狂言|'''{{visible anchor|aikyōgen}}'''|in-between kyōgen, kyōgen interval}}, or as {{Nihongo||別狂言|betsukyōgen|special kyōgen}}.
In aikyōgen, most often the main Noh actor (''shite'') leaves the stage and is replaced by a {{Nihongo|kyōgen actor|狂言方|kyōgen-kata}}, who then explains the play (for the benefit of the audience), though other forms are also possible – the aikyōgen happening at the start, or the kyōgen actor otherwise interacting with the Noh actors. As part of Noh, aikyōgen is ''not'' comic – the manner (movements, way of speech) and costume are serious and dramatic. However, the actor is dressed in a kyōgen outfit and uses kyōgen-style language and delivery (rather than Noh language and delivery) – meaning simpler, less archaic language, delivered closer to a speaking voice – and thus can generally be understood by the audience, hence the role in explaining the play. Thus, while the costume and delivery are kyōgen-''style'' (kyōgen in ''form''), the clothing will be more elegant and the delivery less playful than in separate, comic kyōgen. Before and after aikyōgen, the kyōgen actor waits (kneeling in [[:en:Seiza|Seiza]]) at the {{Nihongo|kyogen seat|狂言座|kyōgen-za}} at the end of the bridge (''hashigakari''), close to the stage.
The traditions of kyōgen are maintained primarily by family groups, especially the [[Izumi school]] and [[:en:Ōkura school|Ōkura school]].
==Elements== Kyōgen plays are invariably brief – often about 10 minutes, as traditionally performed between acts of Noh – and often contain only two or three roles, which are often [[:en:Stock character|Stock character]]s. Notable ones include {{Nihongo||太郎冠者|Tarō kaja|main servant, literally "firstborn son + servant"}}, {{Nihongo||次郎冠者|Jirō kaja|second servant, literally "second son + servant"}}, and {{Nihongo|the master|主人|shujin}}.
Movements and dialogue in kyōgen are typically very exaggerated, making the action of the play easy to understand. Elements of [[:en:slapstick|slapstick]] or [[:en:satire|satire]] are present in most kyōgen plays. Some plays are parodies of actual [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] or [[Shinto]] religious rituals; others are shorter, more lively, simplified versions of Noh plays, many of which are derived from [[:en:Japanese folktales|folktales]]. As with Noh, [[:en:Jo-ha-kyū|Jo-ha-kyū]] is a fundamental principle, which is particularly relevant for movement.
As with Noh and kabuki, all kyōgen [[:en:actor|actor]]s, including those in female roles, are men. Female roles are indicated by a particular piece of attire, a {{Nihongo||美男鬘|binankazura}} – a long white sash, wrapped around the head, with the ends hanging down the front of the body and tucked into the belt, like symbolic braids; at the two points (either side of the head) where the sash changes from being wrapped around to hanging down, the sash sticks up, like two small horns.
Similarly, actors play roles regardless of age – an old man may play the role of Tarō kaja opposite a young man playing master, for instance.
=== Costumes === Outfits are generally [[:en:Kamishimo|Kamishimo]] (Edo period outfit consisting of [[:en:Kataginu|Kataginu]] top and [[:en:Hakama|Hakama]] pants), with the master (if present) generally wearing [[nagabakama]] (long, trailing pants).
Actors in kyōgen, unlike those in Noh, typically do not wear masks, unless the role is that of an animal (such as a [[:en:Bake-danuki|tanuki]] or [[:en:Kitsune|Kitsune]]), or that of a god. Consequently, the masks of kyōgen are less numerous in variety than Noh masks. Both masks and costumes are simpler than those characteristic of Noh. Few props are used, and minimal or no stage sets. As with Noh, a fan is a common accessory.
=== Language === The language in kyōgen depends on the period, but much of the classic repertoire is in [[:en:Early Modern Japanese|Early Modern Japanese]], reasonably analogous to [[:en:Early Modern English|Early Modern English]] (as in [[:en:Shakespeare|Shakespeare]]). The language is largely understandable to contemporary Japanese speakers, but sounds archaic, with pervasive use of the {{Nihongo||ござる|gozaru}} form rather than the {{Nihongo||ます|masu}} form that is now used (see [[Copula (linguistics)#Japanese|copula: Japanese]]). For example, when acknowledging a command, Tarō kaja often replies with {{Nihongo||畏まってござる|kashikomatte-gozaru|"Yes sir!"}}, which in modern Japanese one uses {{Nihongo||畏まりました|kashikomarimashita}}. Further, some of the words and nuances cannot be understood by modern audience (without notes), as in Shakespeare. This contrasts with Noh, where the language is more difficult and generally not understandable to a contemporary audience.
There are numerous set patterns – stock phrases and associated gestures, such as ''kashikomatte-gozaru'' (with a bow) and ''Kore wa mazu nanto itasō. Iya! Itashiyō ga gozaru.'' "So first, what to do. Aha! There is a way to do it.", performed while bowing and cocking head (indicating thought), followed by standing up with a start on ''Iya!'' Plays often begin with set phrases such as ''Kore wa kono atari ni sumai-itasu mono de gozaru.'' "This is the person who resides in this place." and (if featuring Tarō kaja) often end with Tarō kaja running off the stage yelling ''Yaru-mai zo, yaru-mai zo!'' "I won't do it, I won't do it!".
Lines are delivered in a characteristic rhythmic, sing-song voice, and generally quite loudly. Pace, pitch, and volume are all varied for emphasis and effect.
=== Movements === [[File:Noh-stage.jpg|thumb|A contemporary Noh theatre with indoor roofed structure]] As with Noh, which is performed on the same stage, and indeed many martial arts (such as [[:en:Kendo|Kendo]] and [[:en:Aikido|Aikido]]) actors move via {{Nihongo||摺り足|[[suriashi]]}}, sliding their feet, avoiding steps on the easily vibrated Noh stage. When walking, the body seeks to remain at the same level, without bobbing up or down. Plays also frequently feature stamping feet or otherwise hitting the ground (such as jumping) to take advantage of the stage.
As with Noh, angle of gaze is important, and usually a flat gaze is used (avoiding looking down or up, which create a sad or fierce atmosphere, which is to be avoided). Characters usually face each other when speaking, but turn towards the audience when delivering a lengthy speech.
Arms and legs are kept slightly bent. Unless involved in action, hands are kept on upper thighs, with fingers together and thumb tucked in – they move down to the sides of the knees when bowing.
=== Music === Kyōgen is performed to the accompaniment of music, especially the flute, drums, and gong. However, the emphasis of kyōgen is on dialogue and action, rather than on music or dance.
=== Space === Kyogen is generally performed on a Noh stage, as the stage is an important part of the play (the space, the reaction to stamps, the ease of sliding, etc.). It can, however, be performed in any space (particularly by amateur or younger performers), though if possible a Noh-like floor will be installed.
==Komai== In addition to the kyōgen plays themselves, performances include short dances called {{Nihongo||小舞|komai|small dance}}. These are traditional dramatic dances (not comic), performed to a chanted accompaniment, and with varied themes. The movements are broadly similar to Noh dances. The often archaic language used in the lyrics and the chanted delivery means that these chants are often not understandable to a contemporary audience.
==Kyōgen today== Today, kyōgen is performed and practiced regularly, both in major cities (especially Tokyo and Osaka) and throughout the country, and is featured on cultural television programs. In addition to the performances during Noh plays, it is also performed independently, generally in programs of three to five plays.
New kyogen are written regularly, though few new plays enter the repertoire. Particularly significant is {{Nihongo||濯ぎ川|Susugigawa|''The Washing River''}}, written and directed by [[:en:Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki]] in 1953, during his [[Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|post-Kabuki theater work]]. Based on a medieval French farce, this play became the first new ''kyōgen'' to enter the traditional repertoire in a century.<ref>Salz, p.131–136.</ref> In rare cases bilingual kyōgen or fusion of kyōgen with Western forms has been done. An early example is the group ''Mei-no-kai,'' consisting of kyōgen, Noh, and [[:en:shingeki|shingeki]] actors, who staged Beckett's ''[[:en:Waiting for Godot|Waiting for Godot]]'' in 1973; the kyōgen acting was best received.<ref>''The International Reception of Samuel Beckett,'' by Matthew Feldman, "Beckett's Reception in Japan", [https://books.google.com/books?id=cD1B-PzxDckC&pg=PA153 p. 153]</ref> A notable example is the Noho Theatre group, based in Kyoto, under the direction of American Jonah Salz and primary acting by Akira Shigeyama. This group has performed a bilingual Japanese/English translation of ''Susugigawa'' termed ''The Henpecked Husband,'' together with works by [[:en:Samuel Beckett|Samuel Beckett]], notably the mime ''[[:en:Act Without Words I|Act Without Words I]],'' performed by a kyōgen actor in Japanese theatrical style (first performed 1981).<ref name="twist">{{Cite web | title = Noho Theatre: Kyogen with a twist | work = The Japan Times Online | date = Dec 12, 2001 | first = Catherine | last = Pawasarat | access-date = 2012-07-26 | url = http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ft20011212a4.html }}</ref><ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mFkrdBwhvMM Noho Theatre Group ACT WITHOUT WORDS 1], video</ref><ref>"[http://theater.nytimes.com/mem/theater/treview.html?res=9A0DE3DD1538F931A25750C0A960948260 Theater: Beckett, in Japanese Style]", Mel Gussow, ''The New York Times,'' March 12, 1986</ref> This latter features kyōgen movements and Japanese cultural adaptations – for example, the nameless character contemplates suicide not by holding scissors to his throat (as per stage directions), but to his stomach, as if contemplating [[:en:hara-kiri|hara-kiri]]. Unusually for a Beckett adaptation, which are usually strictly controlled by Beckett and his estate, this was presented to Beckett and met with his approval.
The distinctive diction of kyōgen is also occasionally used in other media, with kyōgen actors working as voice actors. An example is the animated movie {{Nihongo|''[[:en:A Country Doctor (film)|A Country Doctor]]''|カフカ 田舎医者|Kafuka: Inaka Isha}} by [[:en:Kōji Yamamura|Kōji Yamamura]], based on "[[:en:A Country Doctor (short story)|A Country Doctor]]" by [[:en:Franz Kafka|Franz Kafka]], where the voices are performed by the Shigeyama family.
As with Noh, many Japanese are familiar with kyōgen only through learning about it in school or television performances. A play frequently featured in textbooks is {{Nihongo||附子|Busu|''The Delicious Poison''}}, where the servants Tarō-kaja and Jirō-kaja are entrusted with some sugar by their master, but told not to eat it, as it is poison; naturally, they eat it. As with Noh, many professional performers are born into a family, often starting performing at a young age, but others are not born into families and beginning practicing in high school or college. Unlike Noh drama or nihonbuyō dance, who earn their living primarily via teaching and support from underlings in the [[:en:Iemoto|Iemoto]] system, but similar to [[rakugo]] comedy, professional kyōgen players earn their living from performing (possibly supplemented by side jobs), and maintain an active touring schedule. Due to the limited repertoire (a classical canon, of which many are no longer performed due to being dated, and few new plays enter) and frequent performances, a professional kyōgen actor can be expected to be familiar with all roles in all plays in their school's repertoire, and to perform them with some regularity.
While there are a number of kyōgen families, there are at present two leading families: the Nomura 野村 family of Tokyo (traditionally Edo region), and the Shigeyama 茂山 family of Kyoto (traditionally [[:en:Kamigata|Kamigata]] region) of the [[:en:Ōkura school|Ōkura school]],<ref name="woodworth">{{Cite web| title = Kyougen: Farce and Folly on the Stage| author = Joseph Woodworth| work = AJET.net - Voice Online| access-date = 2012-07-26| url = http://voice.ajet.net/2010/09/08/kyougen-farce-and-folly-on-the-stage/| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140720134843/http://voice.ajet.net/2010/09/08/kyougen-farce-and-folly-on-the-stage/| archive-date = 2014-07-20}}</ref> both of which are often featured performing on TV, appear in the news, and tour overseas, and have been involved in popularizing and some efforts at modernizing kyōgen.<ref>{{Cite news | issn = 0362-4331| last = Pareles| first = Jon| title = Stage: Nomura Kyogen Theater of Japan| work = The New York Times| access-date = 2012-07-26| date = 1984-07-21| url = https://www.nytimes.com/1984/07/21/arts/stage-nomura-kyogen-theater-of-japan.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title = Revitalized kyogen to a crossroads | work = The Japan Times Online| access-date = 2012-07-26| date = Nov 14, 2001| first = Nobuko| last = Tanaka| url = http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ft20011114a1.html}}</ref> See also the [[:en:List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)|List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)]], whose kyōgen members feature individuals from these families, among others.
=== Foreign actors === In the post-war period, foreigners have participated in kyōgen as amateur performers. A notable early example was the 1956 performance by scholar and translator [[:en:Donald Keene|Donald Keene]] in the play {{Nihongo||千鳥|Chidori|''Plover''}} with [[:en:Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki]] in the role of the [[sake]] shop owner, before an audience including such prominent authors as [[:en:Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|Tanizaki]], [[:en:Yasunari Kawabata|Yasunari Kawabata]] and [[:en:Yukio Mishima|Yukio Mishima]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Keene|first=Donald|author-link=Donald Keene|title=25. Triumph as Tarokaja |url=http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/features/essay/20060708dy02.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20060720051850/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/features/essay/20060708dy02.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 20, 2006|publisher=[[:en:Yomiuri Shimbun|Yomiuri Shimbun]]|date=July 8, 2006|access-date=4 January 2008}}</ref> This is featured in his series of essays, ''Chronicles of My Life in the 20th Century'', and inspired the title of his anthology ''The Blue-Eyed Tarokaja: A Donald Keene Anthology.'' Today foreigners (resident in Japan, with sufficient Japanese skills) are able to practice with amateur troupes.<ref name="woodworth" /> In addition, since 1985, an intensive summer program (originally 6 weeks, now 3 weeks) in kyōgen for beginners has been run at the [[:en:Kyoto Art Center|Kyoto Art Center]], taught by Akira Shigeyama (of the Shigeyama family) and others, and organized by scholar of Japanese theater Jonah Salz.<ref name="twist" /><ref>[https://archive.today/20121219230353/http://en.kac.or.jp/Category:kk]][[Category/46 T.T.T. Category:kk]][[Category] at the [http://en.kac.or.jp/ Kyoto Art Center] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20121219125720/http://en.kac.or.jp/ |date=2012-12-19 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title = Traditional Theatre Training in Kyoto | author = Paura Chan | work = [http://shinpaideshou.wordpress.com/ What can I do with a B.A. in Japanese Studies?] | date = April 5, 2011 | access-date = 2012-07-26 | url = http://shinpaideshou.wordpress.com/2011/04/05/traditional-theatre-training-in-kyoto/}}</ref>
==Plays== There are a few hundred plays in the repertoire (about 180 in the Okura school), but many are now rarely performed, as the audience will not understand the jokes, or would deem them offensive (e.g., for making fun of a blind money-lender).<ref>Don Kenny - The Kyōgen book: an anthology of Japanese classical comedies'' 1989 Demon Plays Asahina (Asahina, the Warrior) Bakuchijuo (A Gambler Beats the King of Hell) Bakuro (Bakuro, the Horse Trainer) Kaminari (Thunder) Kubihiki (Neck Pulling) Oni no Mamako* (The Demon's Stepchild) Seirai (Seirai, the Hawk ...</ref>
Plays commonly studied and performed by beginners, due to brevity and simplicity, include {{Nihongo||痿痢|Shibiri|"Cramps", "Pins and Needles"}}, 舟船, 土筆, 以呂波, and {{Nihongo||口真似|Kuchimane|The Mimic}}.<ref>[http://www.tarokaja.com/wiki.cgi?page=%E1%DF%CE%A1 痿痢]{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ''Shibiri'' "Cramps"</ref> ''Kuchimane'' in particular is frequently performed. Another well-known play, featured in textbooks, is {{Nihongo||附子|Busu|"Wolfsbane", "The Delicious Poison"}}, mentioned above.
Another play is {{Nihongo2|柿山伏}} (''Kakiyamabushi'' or "Persimmon Mountain Hermit"), about an ascetic priest who hungers in the mountains; he uncovers and eats from a persimmon tree, which belongs to a farmer. The farmer catches him in the act and makes a fool out of the priest – getting the priest to pretend to be a crow, a monkey, and a large bird, causing him to fall from the tree. The priest later gets his revenge by chanting and summoning supernatural forces. But in the end, the farmer refuses to nurse the priest back to health.

{{Nihongo|'''''Kyōgen'''''|狂言|extra="mad words" or "wild speech"}} is a form of traditional {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}ese comic [[:en:Theater|Theater]]. It developed alongside ''{{ill|Noh|en|Noh|WD=Q226887|lt=Noh}}'', was performed along with ''Noh'' as an intermission of sorts between ''Noh'' acts on the same stage, and retains close links to ''Noh'' in the modern day; therefore, it is sometimes designated '''''Noh-kyōgen'''''. Its contents are nevertheless not at all similar to the formal, symbolic, and solemn ''Noh'' theater; ''kyōgen'' is a comic form, and its primary goal is to make its audience laugh.
''Kyōgen'' together with ''Noh'' is part of ''{{ill|Nōgaku|en|Nōgaku|WD=Q1037119|lt=Nōgaku}}'' theatre.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/nogaku-theatre-00012|title=Nôgaku theatre - intangible heritage - Culture Sector - UNESCO|website=ich.unesco.org|access-date=29 April 2018}}</ref>
''Kyōgen'' is sometimes compared to the Italian comic form of {{ill|commedia dell'arte|en|commedia dell'arte|WD=Q191890|lt=commedia dell'arte}}<ref>https://journals.library.brandeis.edu%2Findex.php%2FPMAJLS%2Farticle%2Fdownload%2F2351%2F1841%2F5834&psig=AOvVaw3u7L8po-EoB3i6zHVdejYq&ust=1730774138655000&source=images&cd=vfe&opi=89978449&ved=0CAYQrpoMahcKEwjwv7a00sGJAxUAAAAAHQAAAAAQBA</ref>, which developed in the early 17h century, and likewise features {{ill|Stock character|en|Stock character|WD=Q636497|lt=Stock character}}s. It also has parallels with the Greek {{ill|satyr play|en|satyr play|WD=Q1050848|lt=satyr play}}, a short, comical play performed between tragedies.
==History== One of the oldest ancestors of kyogen is considered to be a comical mimicry, which was one of the arts constituting Sangaku ([[:ja:散楽]]), and Sangaku was introduced to Japan from China in the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period}} in the 8th century. In the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}} (794－1185), sangaku developed into {{ill|Sarugaku|en|Sarugaku|WD=Q1204318|lt=Sarugaku}} by merging with Japanese traditional performing arts such as {{ill|Dengaku|en|Dengaku|WD=Q3022455|lt=Dengaku}}, and in the {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}} (1185－1333), it was divided into Noh, which was a drama of serious singing and dancing, and kyogen, which was a comical speech and play. When {{ill|Kan'ami|en|Kan'ami|WD=Q1291653|lt=Kan'ami}} and {{ill|Zeami Motokiyo|en|Zeami Motokiyo|WD=Q169352|lt=Zeami}} completed Noh in the style known today in the early {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} (1333－1573) in the 14th century, Kyōgen was a simple and comical short play different from the style known today, and performers of kyōgen were under the control of a Noh troupe. In the late Muromachi period, kyōgen as a form of theater was developed and the {{ill|Ōkura school|en|Ōkura school|WD=Q8081585|lt=Ōkura school}} was established by kyōgen performers. In the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} (1606－1868), Sagi school and Izumi school were established. Since the [[Tokugawa shogunate]] designated kyōgen and Noh as ceremonial arts in the Edo period, kyōgen performers of these three schools were employed by the Tokugawa shogunate, each [[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]] (feudal lord) and the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|WD=Q909452|lt=Imperial Court}}, and kyōgen also developed greatly.<ref name = "kotobank">[https://web.archive.org/web/20210427204341/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%8B%82%E8%A8%80-52582 Kotobank, ''Kyōgen''.] {{ill|The Asahi Shimbun|en|The Asahi Shimbun|WD=Q720503|lt=The Asahi Shimbun}}</ref>
Kyōgen provided a major influence on the later development of {{ill|Kabuki|en|Kabuki|WD=Q199701|lt=Kabuki}} theater. After the earlier, more ribald forms of kabuki had been outlawed in the mid-17th century, the government permitted the establishment of the new ''yarō-kabuki'' (men's kabuki) only on the grounds that it refrain from the previous kabuki forms' lewdness and instead model itself after kyōgen.<ref name = "kotobank"/>
Noh had been the official entertainment form of the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, and was therefore subsidized by the government. Kyōgen, performed in conjunction with Noh, also received the patronage of the government and the upper class during this time. Following the [[Meiji Restoration]], however, this support ceased. Without government support, Noh and kyōgen went into decline, as many Japanese citizens gravitated toward the more "modern" Western art forms. In 1879, however, then-former {{ill|President of the United States|en|President of the United States|WD=Q11696|lt=US President}} {{ill|Ulysses S. Grant|en|Ulysses S. Grant|WD=Q34836|lt=Ulysses S. Grant}} and his wife, while touring Japan, expressed an interest in the traditional art of Noh. They became the first {{ill|United States|en|United States|WD=Q30|lt=Americans}} to witness Noh and kyōgen plays and are said to have enjoyed the performance. Their approval is believed to have sparked a revival of interest in these forms.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.prweb.com/releases/2004/11/prweb182046.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041223132719/http://www.prweb.com/releases/2004/11/prweb182046.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 23, 2004 |title="First Noh & Kyogen Program Witnessed by Americans" in Boston December 7, 2004. |date= 25 November 2004 |publisher=PRWeb |access-date=31 May 2010}}</ref>
In modern Japan, kyōgen is performed both separately and as a part of Noh. When performed as part of a Noh performance, kyōgen can take three forms: a separate (comic) kyōgen play, performed between two Noh plays (inter-Noh), which is known as {{Nihongo||本狂言|honkyōgen|actual kyōgen}}, as a (non-comic) scene ''within'' a Noh play (intra-Noh, between two scenes), which is known as {{Nihongo||間狂言|'''{{visible anchor|aikyōgen}}'''|in-between kyōgen, kyōgen interval}}, or as {{Nihongo||別狂言|betsukyōgen|special kyōgen}}.
In aikyōgen, most often the main Noh actor (''shite'') leaves the stage and is replaced by a {{Nihongo|kyōgen actor|狂言方|kyōgen-kata}}, who then explains the play (for the benefit of the audience), though other forms are also possible – the aikyōgen happening at the start, or the kyōgen actor otherwise interacting with the Noh actors. As part of Noh, aikyōgen is ''not'' comic – the manner (movements, way of speech) and costume are serious and dramatic. However, the actor is dressed in a kyōgen outfit and uses kyōgen-style language and delivery (rather than Noh language and delivery) – meaning simpler, less archaic language, delivered closer to a speaking voice – and thus can generally be understood by the audience, hence the role in explaining the play. Thus, while the costume and delivery are kyōgen-''style'' (kyōgen in ''form''), the clothing will be more elegant and the delivery less playful than in separate, comic kyōgen. Before and after aikyōgen, the kyōgen actor waits (kneeling in {{ill|Seiza|en|Seiza|WD=Q1426744|lt=Seiza}}) at the {{Nihongo|kyogen seat|狂言座|kyōgen-za}} at the end of the bridge (''hashigakari''), close to the stage.
The traditions of kyōgen are maintained primarily by family groups, especially the [[Izumi school]] and {{ill|Ōkura school|en|Ōkura school|WD=Q8081585|lt=Ōkura school}}.
==Elements== Kyōgen plays are invariably brief – often about 10 minutes, as traditionally performed between acts of Noh – and often contain only two or three roles, which are often {{ill|Stock character|en|Stock character|WD=Q636497|lt=Stock character}}s. Notable ones include {{Nihongo||太郎冠者|Tarō kaja|main servant, literally "firstborn son + servant"}}, {{Nihongo||次郎冠者|Jirō kaja|second servant, literally "second son + servant"}}, and {{Nihongo|the master|主人|shujin}}.
Movements and dialogue in kyōgen are typically very exaggerated, making the action of the play easy to understand. Elements of {{ill|slapstick|en|slapstick|WD=Q624771|lt=slapstick}} or {{ill|satire|en|satire|WD=Q128758|lt=satire}} are present in most kyōgen plays. Some plays are parodies of actual {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism}} or [[Shinto]] religious rituals; others are shorter, more lively, simplified versions of Noh plays, many of which are derived from {{ill|Japanese folktales|en|Japanese folktales|WD=Q2349495|lt=folktales}}. As with Noh, {{ill|Jo-ha-kyū|en|Jo-ha-kyū|WD=Q6204009|lt=Jo-ha-kyū}} is a fundamental principle, which is particularly relevant for movement.
As with Noh and kabuki, all kyōgen {{ill|actor|en|actor|WD=Q33999|lt=actor}}s, including those in female roles, are men. Female roles are indicated by a particular piece of attire, a {{Nihongo||美男鬘|binankazura}} – a long white sash, wrapped around the head, with the ends hanging down the front of the body and tucked into the belt, like symbolic braids; at the two points (either side of the head) where the sash changes from being wrapped around to hanging down, the sash sticks up, like two small horns.
Similarly, actors play roles regardless of age – an old man may play the role of Tarō kaja opposite a young man playing master, for instance.
=== Costumes === Outfits are generally [[:en:Kamishimo|Kamishimo]] (Edo period outfit consisting of [[:en:Kataginu|Kataginu]] top and {{ill|Hakama|en|Hakama|WD=Q164668|lt=Hakama}} pants), with the master (if present) generally wearing [[nagabakama]] (long, trailing pants).
Actors in kyōgen, unlike those in Noh, typically do not wear masks, unless the role is that of an animal (such as a {{ill|Bake-danuki|en|Bake-danuki|WD=Q1771860|lt=tanuki}} or {{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Kitsune}}), or that of a god. Consequently, the masks of kyōgen are less numerous in variety than Noh masks. Both masks and costumes are simpler than those characteristic of Noh. Few props are used, and minimal or no stage sets. As with Noh, a fan is a common accessory.
=== Language === The language in kyōgen depends on the period, but much of the classic repertoire is in {{ill|Early Modern Japanese|en|Early Modern Japanese|WD=Q5326692|lt=Early Modern Japanese}}, reasonably analogous to {{ill|Early Modern English|en|Early Modern English|WD=Q1472196|lt=Early Modern English}} (as in [[:en:Shakespeare|Shakespeare]]). The language is largely understandable to contemporary Japanese speakers, but sounds archaic, with pervasive use of the {{Nihongo||ござる|gozaru}} form rather than the {{Nihongo||ます|masu}} form that is now used (see [[Copula (linguistics)#Japanese|copula: Japanese]]). For example, when acknowledging a command, Tarō kaja often replies with {{Nihongo||畏まってござる|kashikomatte-gozaru|"Yes sir!"}}, which in modern Japanese one uses {{Nihongo||畏まりました|kashikomarimashita}}. Further, some of the words and nuances cannot be understood by modern audience (without notes), as in Shakespeare. This contrasts with Noh, where the language is more difficult and generally not understandable to a contemporary audience.
There are numerous set patterns – stock phrases and associated gestures, such as ''kashikomatte-gozaru'' (with a bow) and ''Kore wa mazu nanto itasō. Iya! Itashiyō ga gozaru.'' "So first, what to do. Aha! There is a way to do it.", performed while bowing and cocking head (indicating thought), followed by standing up with a start on ''Iya!'' Plays often begin with set phrases such as ''Kore wa kono atari ni sumai-itasu mono de gozaru.'' "This is the person who resides in this place." and (if featuring Tarō kaja) often end with Tarō kaja running off the stage yelling ''Yaru-mai zo, yaru-mai zo!'' "I won't do it, I won't do it!".
Lines are delivered in a characteristic rhythmic, sing-song voice, and generally quite loudly. Pace, pitch, and volume are all varied for emphasis and effect.
=== Movements === [[File:Noh-stage.jpg|thumb|A contemporary Noh theatre with indoor roofed structure]] As with Noh, which is performed on the same stage, and indeed many martial arts (such as {{ill|Kendo|en|Kendo|WD=Q170931|lt=Kendo}} and {{ill|Aikido|en|Aikido|WD=Q43114|lt=Aikido}}) actors move via {{Nihongo||摺り足|[[suriashi]]}}, sliding their feet, avoiding steps on the easily vibrated Noh stage. When walking, the body seeks to remain at the same level, without bobbing up or down. Plays also frequently feature stamping feet or otherwise hitting the ground (such as jumping) to take advantage of the stage.
As with Noh, angle of gaze is important, and usually a flat gaze is used (avoiding looking down or up, which create a sad or fierce atmosphere, which is to be avoided). Characters usually face each other when speaking, but turn towards the audience when delivering a lengthy speech.
Arms and legs are kept slightly bent. Unless involved in action, hands are kept on upper thighs, with fingers together and thumb tucked in – they move down to the sides of the knees when bowing.
=== Music === Kyōgen is performed to the accompaniment of music, especially the flute, drums, and gong. However, the emphasis of kyōgen is on dialogue and action, rather than on music or dance.
=== Space === Kyogen is generally performed on a Noh stage, as the stage is an important part of the play (the space, the reaction to stamps, the ease of sliding, etc.). It can, however, be performed in any space (particularly by amateur or younger performers), though if possible a Noh-like floor will be installed.
==Komai== In addition to the kyōgen plays themselves, performances include short dances called {{Nihongo||小舞|komai|small dance}}. These are traditional dramatic dances (not comic), performed to a chanted accompaniment, and with varied themes. The movements are broadly similar to Noh dances. The often archaic language used in the lyrics and the chanted delivery means that these chants are often not understandable to a contemporary audience.
==Kyōgen today== Today, kyōgen is performed and practiced regularly, both in major cities (especially Tokyo and Osaka) and throughout the country, and is featured on cultural television programs. In addition to the performances during Noh plays, it is also performed independently, generally in programs of three to five plays.
New kyogen are written regularly, though few new plays enter the repertoire. Particularly significant is {{Nihongo||濯ぎ川|Susugigawa|''The Washing River''}}, written and directed by {{ill|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|en|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|WD=Q7706872|lt=Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki}} in 1953, during his [[Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|post-Kabuki theater work]]. Based on a medieval French farce, this play became the first new ''kyōgen'' to enter the traditional repertoire in a century.<ref>Salz, p.131–136.</ref> In rare cases bilingual kyōgen or fusion of kyōgen with Western forms has been done. An early example is the group ''Mei-no-kai,'' consisting of kyōgen, Noh, and {{ill|shingeki|en|shingeki|WD=Q3482195|lt=shingeki}} actors, who staged Beckett's ''{{ill|Waiting for Godot|en|Waiting for Godot|WD=Q19871|lt=Waiting for Godot}}'' in 1973; the kyōgen acting was best received.<ref>''The International Reception of Samuel Beckett,'' by Matthew Feldman, "Beckett's Reception in Japan", [https://books.google.com/books?id=cD1B-PzxDckC&pg=PA153 p. 153]</ref> A notable example is the Noho Theatre group, based in Kyoto, under the direction of American Jonah Salz and primary acting by Akira Shigeyama. This group has performed a bilingual Japanese/English translation of ''Susugigawa'' termed ''The Henpecked Husband,'' together with works by {{ill|Samuel Beckett|en|Samuel Beckett|WD=Q37327|lt=Samuel Beckett}}, notably the mime ''{{ill|Act Without Words I|en|Act Without Words I|WD=Q421763|lt=Act Without Words I}},'' performed by a kyōgen actor in Japanese theatrical style (first performed 1981).<ref name="twist">{{Cite web | title = Noho Theatre: Kyogen with a twist | work = The Japan Times Online | date = Dec 12, 2001 | first = Catherine | last = Pawasarat | access-date = 2012-07-26 | url = http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ft20011212a4.html }}</ref><ref>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mFkrdBwhvMM Noho Theatre Group ACT WITHOUT WORDS 1], video</ref><ref>"[http://theater.nytimes.com/mem/theater/treview.html?res=9A0DE3DD1538F931A25750C0A960948260 Theater: Beckett, in Japanese Style]", Mel Gussow, ''The New York Times,'' March 12, 1986</ref> This latter features kyōgen movements and Japanese cultural adaptations – for example, the nameless character contemplates suicide not by holding scissors to his throat (as per stage directions), but to his stomach, as if contemplating [[:en:hara-kiri|hara-kiri]]. Unusually for a Beckett adaptation, which are usually strictly controlled by Beckett and his estate, this was presented to Beckett and met with his approval.
The distinctive diction of kyōgen is also occasionally used in other media, with kyōgen actors working as voice actors. An example is the animated movie {{Nihongo|''{{ill|A Country Doctor (film)|en|A Country Doctor (film)|WD=Q4656141|lt=A Country Doctor}}''|カフカ 田舎医者|Kafuka: Inaka Isha}} by {{ill|Kōji Yamamura|en|Kōji Yamamura|WD=Q921662|lt=Kōji Yamamura}}, based on "{{ill|A Country Doctor (short story)|en|A Country Doctor (short story)|WD=Q1304771|lt=A Country Doctor}}" by {{ill|Franz Kafka|en|Franz Kafka|WD=Q905|lt=Franz Kafka}}, where the voices are performed by the Shigeyama family.
As with Noh, many Japanese are familiar with kyōgen only through learning about it in school or television performances. A play frequently featured in textbooks is {{Nihongo||附子|Busu|''The Delicious Poison''}}, where the servants Tarō-kaja and Jirō-kaja are entrusted with some sugar by their master, but told not to eat it, as it is poison; naturally, they eat it. As with Noh, many professional performers are born into a family, often starting performing at a young age, but others are not born into families and beginning practicing in high school or college. Unlike Noh drama or nihonbuyō dance, who earn their living primarily via teaching and support from underlings in the {{ill|Iemoto|en|Iemoto|WD=Q2404873|lt=Iemoto}} system, but similar to [[rakugo]] comedy, professional kyōgen players earn their living from performing (possibly supplemented by side jobs), and maintain an active touring schedule. Due to the limited repertoire (a classical canon, of which many are no longer performed due to being dated, and few new plays enter) and frequent performances, a professional kyōgen actor can be expected to be familiar with all roles in all plays in their school's repertoire, and to perform them with some regularity.
While there are a number of kyōgen families, there are at present two leading families: the Nomura 野村 family of Tokyo (traditionally Edo region), and the Shigeyama 茂山 family of Kyoto (traditionally {{ill|Kamigata|en|Kamigata|WD=Q403130|lt=Kamigata}} region) of the {{ill|Ōkura school|en|Ōkura school|WD=Q8081585|lt=Ōkura school}},<ref name="woodworth">{{Cite web| title = Kyougen: Farce and Folly on the Stage| author = Joseph Woodworth| work = AJET.net - Voice Online| access-date = 2012-07-26| url = http://voice.ajet.net/2010/09/08/kyougen-farce-and-folly-on-the-stage/| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140720134843/http://voice.ajet.net/2010/09/08/kyougen-farce-and-folly-on-the-stage/| archive-date = 2014-07-20}}</ref> both of which are often featured performing on TV, appear in the news, and tour overseas, and have been involved in popularizing and some efforts at modernizing kyōgen.<ref>{{Cite news | issn = 0362-4331| last = Pareles| first = Jon| title = Stage: Nomura Kyogen Theater of Japan| work = The New York Times| access-date = 2012-07-26| date = 1984-07-21| url = https://www.nytimes.com/1984/07/21/arts/stage-nomura-kyogen-theater-of-japan.html}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title = Revitalized kyogen to a crossroads | work = The Japan Times Online| access-date = 2012-07-26| date = Nov 14, 2001| first = Nobuko| last = Tanaka| url = http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/ft20011114a1.html}}</ref> See also the {{ill|List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)|en|List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)|WD=Q6576958|lt=List of Living National Treasures of Japan (performing arts)}}, whose kyōgen members feature individuals from these families, among others.
=== Foreign actors === In the post-war period, foreigners have participated in kyōgen as amateur performers. A notable early example was the 1956 performance by scholar and translator {{ill|Donald Keene|en|Donald Keene|WD=Q1240040|lt=Donald Keene}} in the play {{Nihongo||千鳥|Chidori|''Plover''}} with {{ill|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|en|Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki|WD=Q7706872|lt=Tetsuji Takechi#Theater work after Takechi Kabuki}} in the role of the [[sake]] shop owner, before an audience including such prominent authors as {{ill|Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|en|Jun'ichirō Tanizaki|WD=Q316213|lt=Tanizaki}}, {{ill|Yasunari Kawabata|en|Yasunari Kawabata|WD=Q43736|lt=Yasunari Kawabata}} and {{ill|Yukio Mishima|en|Yukio Mishima|WD=Q134456|lt=Yukio Mishima}}.<ref>{{cite news |last=Keene|first=Donald|author-link=Donald Keene|title=25. Triumph as Tarokaja |url=http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/features/essay/20060708dy02.htm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20060720051850/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/features/essay/20060708dy02.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 20, 2006|publisher={{ill|Yomiuri Shimbun|en|Yomiuri Shimbun|WD=Q645218|lt=Yomiuri Shimbun}}|date=July 8, 2006|access-date=4 January 2008}}</ref> This is featured in his series of essays, ''Chronicles of My Life in the 20th Century'', and inspired the title of his anthology ''The Blue-Eyed Tarokaja: A Donald Keene Anthology.'' Today foreigners (resident in Japan, with sufficient Japanese skills) are able to practice with amateur troupes.<ref name="woodworth" /> In addition, since 1985, an intensive summer program (originally 6 weeks, now 3 weeks) in kyōgen for beginners has been run at the {{ill|Kyoto Art Center|en|Kyoto Art Center|WD=Q6452114|lt=Kyoto Art Center}}, taught by Akira Shigeyama (of the Shigeyama family) and others, and organized by scholar of Japanese theater Jonah Salz.<ref name="twist" /><ref>[https://archive.today/20121219230353/http://en.kac.or.jp/Category:kk]][[Category/46 T.T.T. Category:kk]][[Category] at the [http://en.kac.or.jp/ Kyoto Art Center] {{webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20121219125720/http://en.kac.or.jp/ |date=2012-12-19 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title = Traditional Theatre Training in Kyoto | author = Paura Chan | work = [http://shinpaideshou.wordpress.com/ What can I do with a B.A. in Japanese Studies?] | date = April 5, 2011 | access-date = 2012-07-26 | url = http://shinpaideshou.wordpress.com/2011/04/05/traditional-theatre-training-in-kyoto/}}</ref>
==Plays== There are a few hundred plays in the repertoire (about 180 in the Okura school), but many are now rarely performed, as the audience will not understand the jokes, or would deem them offensive (e.g., for making fun of a blind money-lender).<ref>Don Kenny - The Kyōgen book: an anthology of Japanese classical comedies'' 1989 Demon Plays Asahina (Asahina, the Warrior) Bakuchijuo (A Gambler Beats the King of Hell) Bakuro (Bakuro, the Horse Trainer) Kaminari (Thunder) Kubihiki (Neck Pulling) Oni no Mamako* (The Demon's Stepchild) Seirai (Seirai, the Hawk ...</ref>
Plays commonly studied and performed by beginners, due to brevity and simplicity, include {{Nihongo||痿痢|Shibiri|"Cramps", "Pins and Needles"}}, 舟船, 土筆, 以呂波, and {{Nihongo||口真似|Kuchimane|The Mimic}}.<ref>[http://www.tarokaja.com/wiki.cgi?page=%E1%DF%CE%A1 痿痢]{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} ''Shibiri'' "Cramps"</ref> ''Kuchimane'' in particular is frequently performed. Another well-known play, featured in textbooks, is {{Nihongo||附子|Busu|"Wolfsbane", "The Delicious Poison"}}, mentioned above.
Another play is {{Nihongo2|柿山伏}} (''Kakiyamabushi'' or "Persimmon Mountain Hermit"), about an ascetic priest who hungers in the mountains; he uncovers and eats from a persimmon tree, which belongs to a farmer. The farmer catches him in the act and makes a fool out of the priest – getting the priest to pretend to be a crow, a monkey, and a large bird, causing him to fall from the tree. The priest later gets his revenge by chanting and summoning supernatural forces. But in the end, the farmer refuses to nurse the priest back to health.
